topics.title: Who was Florence Nightingale?
topics.intro: Florence Nightingale was born more than 200 years ago, into a rich family. Rich girls were not expected to have jobs, but Florence wanted to be a nurse. She would not give up, and in the end she changed hospitals for ever.
topics.teach: Explain why Florence’s family did not want her to be a nurse, and what she did about it.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} would like to be when {she} grows up, and what {she} would do if someone said no.
topics.hook: Florence was born in Florence: her parents named her after the Italian city.

visual.caption: Florence Nightingale lived from 1820 to 1910, through all of Queen Victoria’s reign.

topics.title: The Crimean War and the hospital at Scutari
topics.intro: In 1854 Britain was at war with Russia, far away in the Crimea, by the Black Sea. Many soldiers fell ill and were sent to a big army hospital at Scutari. It was dirty and crowded, so Florence took a team of nurses to help.
topics.teach: Explain what was wrong with the hospital at Scutari, and three things Florence and her nurses did to make it better.
topics.talk: When {she} washes {her} hands before tea, ask {him} why Florence Nightingale would approve.
topics.hook: Say it: Scutari is SKOO-tuh-ree and the Crimea is cry-MEE-uh.

steps: Soldiers fall ill in the Crimea

topics.title: Mary Seacole too
topics.intro: Mary Seacole was born in Jamaica in 1805. Her mother taught her to heal people with medicines made from plants. When the Crimean War began, Mary wanted to help the soldiers. She was not chosen to go, so she went anyway and paid for the journey herself!
topics.teach: Explain one way Mary Seacole and Florence Nightingale were alike, and one way they were different.
topics.talk: Find Jamaica, London and the Black Sea on a map or globe with {him}. How far did Mary travel?
topics.hook: Mary from Jamaica, Florence from Florence: two brave women, one war.

topics.title: Stories from the Crimean War
topics.intro: Three short stories based on true events: young Florence, a soldier in the hospital at Scutari, and a cold soldier who visits Mary Seacole. Read each one carefully, then be a history detective: what do the clues tell you?
topics.teach: Tell your grown-up which story you liked best, and one clue that showed how a person felt.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why {she} thinks the soldiers loved Florence and Mary so much.

topics.title: Counting to save lives: Florence’s rose diagram
topics.intro: Florence loved numbers. She counted how many soldiers died, and what they died of. Then she turned her numbers into pictures, so that busy people could see the problem at a glance. Her most famous picture looks a little like a rose.
topics.teach: Explain what the blue parts of Florence’s rose diagram showed, and why her picture helped persuade people to make hospitals cleaner.
topics.talk: Keep a tally of the weather for a week together, then draw it as a bar chart. Ask {him} what the chart shows at a glance.
topics.hook: Big blue wedges meant a big problem: illnesses that could have been stopped.

visual.caption: Florence’s rose diagram (1858) had two roses: the war’s first year, and the year after the hospitals were cleaned up. The second was much smaller.

topics.title: After the war: a school for nurses
topics.intro: Florence came home from the war a hero, but she did not want parties. For the rest of her long life she worked to make hospitals safer and to turn nursing into a proper job, with training.
topics.teach: Explain how Florence changed nursing after the war, and how we still remember her today.
topics.talk: On 12 May (International Nurses Day), ask {him} to think of a nurse {she} could say thank you to.
topics.hook: A book in 1859, a school in 1860: _Notes on Nursing_, then the Nightingale School.

topics.title: Then and now: hospitals and nursing
topics.intro: Hospitals in Victorian times were very different from hospitals today. Some of the biggest changes began with Florence’s ideas about cleanliness and training. How do we know what her hospitals were like? From clues the past has left behind.
topics.teach: Explain three ways hospitals today are different from Florence’s hospital, and one way they are the same.
topics.talk: If {she} has visited a doctor or a hospital, ask {him} what was clean, what the nurses wore and what machines {she} saw.
topics.hook: Then: lanterns, buckets and scrubbing brushes. Now: electric lights, machines and hand gel.

topics.title: Stories: a clever picture and a museum visit
topics.intro: Two more stories: how Florence turned numbers into a picture that changed people’s minds, and a girl who visits the Florence Nightingale Museum with her grandma. Find the clues, then answer.
topics.teach: Tell your grown-up how we know about Florence today: name two clues from the past.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which object from Florence’s life {she} would most like to see in a museum, and why.

items.passage:
The Girl Who Would Not Give Up

Florence Nightingale grew up in a big house with servants, horses and beautiful gardens. Her parents expected her to go to parties, marry a rich man and never have a job.

But Florence wanted something different. She liked visiting poor families in the village when they were ill, and she was good at caring for them. When she was in her twenties, she told her family that she wanted to be a nurse.

Her mother was horrified. Her sister cried. In those days hospitals were dirty places, and nurses had no proper training. It was not thought a suitable job for a lady.

Florence did not give up. Every morning she woke before dawn, while the house was still quiet, and read reports about hospitals by candlelight. She filled notebooks with facts and numbers.

Year after year, she kept asking. At last, when she was 30, she visited a hospital and nursing school at Kaiserswerth in Germany. The next year she went back to train there. Now Florence felt she was doing the work she was born to do.

items.passage:
The Girl Who Would Not Give Up

Florence Nightingale grew up in a big house with servants, horses and beautiful gardens. Her parents expected her to go to parties, marry a rich man and never have a job.

But Florence wanted something different. She liked visiting poor families in the village when they were ill, and she was good at caring for them. When she was in her twenties, she told her family that she wanted to be a nurse.

Her mother was horrified. Her sister cried. In those days hospitals were dirty places, and nurses had no proper training. It was not thought a suitable job for a lady.

Florence did not give up. Every morning she woke before dawn, while the house was still quiet, and read reports about hospitals by candlelight. She filled notebooks with facts and numbers.

Year after year, she kept asking. At last, when she was 30, she visited a hospital and nursing school at Kaiserswerth in Germany. The next year she went back to train there. Now Florence felt she was doing the work she was born to do.

The Lamp in the Night

Private Tom Reed had never felt so ill. He lay on a thin mattress in the army hospital at Scutari, squashed between two other soldiers. The floor was filthy, and he could hear rats scurrying in the dark.

Then the nurses came.

They arrived with buckets, soap and scrubbing brushes. In charge was a slim, quiet lady in a plain black dress. She did not shout, but everyone did what she said. Her name was Miss Nightingale.

Soon the floor was scrubbed clean. Tom had a clean shirt for the first time in weeks. A nurse brought him warm soup and held the cup while he drank.

At night, when the doctors had gone to bed, a soft light moved slowly along the ward. It was Miss Nightingale, carrying a little Turkish lantern. She stopped at each bed. She tucked in a blanket here and spoke a kind word there.

When her shadow passed over him, Tom smiled. He wrote to his mother: “She makes us feel that somebody cares.”

Tom grew stronger every day. By the spring, he was well enough to go home.

Mother Seacole’s Hotel

Corporal Jack Lewis stamped his frozen feet. It was winter in the Crimea, and the army camp was cold and muddy.

“Come to Mother Seacole’s,” said his friend. “She’ll warm you up.”

On a little hill stood a building made of old planks and sheets of iron. A painted sign said British Hotel. Inside, it was warm and smelled of hot stew and fresh bread. Soldiers sat at the tables, laughing.

Behind the counter stood a smiling woman in a bright dress and bonnet. She had been born in Jamaica, and she had paid for her long journey to the Crimea herself.

“You look poorly, young man,” she said, and handed Jack a steaming drink made from herbs. “Drink that up.”

Later, Jack saw Mrs Seacole ride out towards the battlefield, her bags full of bandages, medicines and food. She did not seem afraid at all.

“Why does she do it?” Jack asked.

His friend smiled. “Because she cares about every one of us. That’s why we call her Mother.”

The Picture That Changed Minds

Florence came home from the war in 1856, but she could not stop thinking about the soldiers who had died. Most of them had not been killed in battle. They had died of illnesses that spread in dirty, crowded hospitals.

Florence was sure that clean hospitals could save thousands of lives. But many important men would not listen.

So Florence did what she was best at. She collected numbers. Month by month, she counted how many soldiers had died, and why. She worked with a clever doctor called William Farr, who loved numbers as much as she did.

Then she had an idea. Long lists of numbers were dull, and busy people did not read them. What if she turned the numbers into a picture?

She drew a circle cut into twelve wedges, one for each month, like the petals of a flower. She coloured the deaths from illnesses that could have been prevented in blue. The blue wedges were huge. The red wedges, for deaths from wounds, were much smaller.

Anyone could see the problem at a glance. Her picture helped persuade the government to make army hospitals cleaner and healthier.

Ellie’s Visit to the Museum

Ellie’s grandma had been a nurse for forty years, so for Ellie’s seventh birthday they went to the Florence Nightingale Museum in London.

The first thing Ellie saw was a lantern. It was not shiny like the lamp in her storybook. It was a plain folding Turkish lantern, and once a candle had glowed inside it.

“Florence carried a lantern like this round the wards at night,” said Grandma.

Next they saw a little owl in a glass case. “That’s Athena,” said Grandma. “Florence rescued her in Greece and carried her about in her pocket.”

Ellie giggled. Then she stopped beside some old letters with spidery handwriting. “Did Florence write these?”

“Yes. She wrote thousands of letters. That’s one way we know so much about her.”

On the way out, they walked through the hospital. Outside a ward, a nurse in a blue uniform was rubbing gel on his hands before he went to see a patient.

“Look, Grandma,” said Ellie. “He’s doing what Florence wanted. Keeping everything clean!”

Grandma smiled. “Lots of things have changed since Florence’s time,” she said, “but caring for people hasn’t.”
